WDFW creel and catch reports

Where Washington is catching fish, and where it stopped

Every creel report WDFW publishes — the statewide interview database, the Puget Sound ramp counts, Buoy 10, Willapa Bay, the ocean quota report, the Columbia River weekly summaries and the pikeminnow reward fishery — read into one record of who fished, where, and what they caught.

How it shifts as the window shortens

A cell is the catch rate over that window, ending on the same day. Reading a row left to right is reading the season tightening down to this past week: a place whose rate climbs as the window shortens is turning on now, one that falls has already had its run. Rates resting on fewer than anglers are marked thin — over seven days most places are.

Best places in the window

Puget Sound Chinook, against the guideline

How much of each quota has been used. These fisheries are managed on encounters rather than on catch, so the figure counted against the guideline is encounters or harvest, whichever WDFW set for that area. An area can run two guideline fisheries in a season, so each is listed under the day it opened. Only areas with a quota appear — this is a measure of quota used, not a statement about whether water is open, which is set by the sport fishing rules.

WDFW state the date each estimate runs through, and that date, not today's, is how current the figure is.

Ocean salmon, by port

Chinook run against a guideline and coho against a quota, and they run out at different times: a port can be most of the way through its Chinook and barely into its coho. Where WDFW publish the share used but not the ceiling, the ceiling is worked back out of their own two figures and rounded, so it is an implied number rather than a published one.

Pacific halibut, by subarea

The only quota here counted in pounds rather than fish.

Where these come from

Read from four WDFW pages: the seasonal salmon fishery guidelines, the ocean sport quota report, the halibut seasons and quotas page, and the white sturgeon page. None of it is creel catch, so none of it is mixed into the catch tables anywhere else in this dashboard.

What is not read

One entry on WDFW's creel index carries no in-season data: Sport catch reports, the annual catch-record-card publications, whose most recent edition covers 2021. They summarise a year rather than track a season, so nothing on this page is built from them. Everything else WDFW lists there is read, including the two quota trackers on the previous tab.

How current each source is

The date of the most recent report read from each source, and how long ago that was. A source that runs a season — Buoy 10 opens in August, Willapa in August, the pikeminnow fishery in spring — is not stale between seasons; it has simply not published yet.

How a number gets here

Every figure is parsed from a WDFW report and nothing is estimated — which also means these are interviewed fish, not a river's total catch. A creel sampler works some days and not others and speaks to some parties and not all, so 2,158 steelhead on the Hoh is what samplers saw in 3,025 interviews over 260 sampled days, not what the river gave up. WDFW's own expanded estimates of total catch are a separate product and are not published in these tables. Catch and effort are kept in separate tables, because one interview counts anglers once and their fish once per species; folding them together would inflate every catch-per-angler figure. Every place that reported fishing is shown, but a rate resting on fewer than anglers is marked thin, drawn faded, and never ranked in the heating and cooling lists — one lucky boat moves a six-angler rate by half. Where a Where WDFW publish the interviews one by one — the statewide database does, the weekly summaries do not — the share of parties that caught one is counted from those interviews rather than estimated from the average catch. Other dashboards model it with a Poisson assumption, which treats fish as arriving independently; they do not, and the modelled number reads high on slow days and low on good ones. Where the interviews were never published, this column says so instead of guessing. Where a report records whether a fish was fin-clipped, that split is carried too: hatchery and wild are not the same fish to a biologist, and under mark-selective rules they are not the same fish to an angler either.
